vignette:
Rodrigo Mendes is a 53-year-old divorced Latino man who works as a tax consultant and presented for psychological evaluation following a traumatic encounter with law enforcement that occurred approximately fourteen months ago. He came to the intake appointment alone, dressed carefully but moving with a guardedness that became more apparent as the session progressed - pausing before sitting, positioning his chair so his back was against the wall, and noting, almost reflexively, where the office door was located.

The incident occurred on a Saturday evening when Rodrigo was returning from a client dinner in an unfamiliar part of the city. He was stopped by two officers who, within moments of approaching his vehicle, escalated the encounter with little apparent provocation. What followed involved Rodrigo being forcibly removed from the car, thrown against the hood, and struck repeatedly - first on his lower back and then across his left forearm as he raised it instinctively. He was left with a fractured radius and bruising across his ribs. He lay on the pavement for several minutes before an ambulance arrived, during which time he could see another man nearby - a bystander who had also been struck - slumped against a wall with blood visible across his face. Rodrigo could not tell whether the man was conscious. That image, he said, was the one that came back to him most often.

In the months that followed, Rodrigo's world contracted. The fracture healed imperfectly, and even now a dull ache persists in his forearm, particularly in cold weather or when he types for extended periods - which, as a tax consultant working through filing season, is nearly constant. Each flare of that pain arrives not only as a physical sensation but as something that pulls him back to the pavement, to the weight of the officer's knee, to the sound of the other man's laboured breathing. He has come to dread the physical discomfort in a way that goes beyond ordinary pain aversion, because for Rodrigo the sensation and the memory are inseparable.

His work has suffered in ways that are now difficult to conceal. Tax consultation requires site visits to new clients - offices in unfamiliar buildings, parking structures he has never navigated before. Rodrigo now declines these appointments, citing scheduling conflicts, and has lost two significant corporate accounts as a result. When he does enter any new environment, he spends the first several minutes identifying exits before he can attend to anything else, and he checks over his shoulder with a frequency that colleagues have begun to notice and comment on. A junior associate asked him last month whether something was wrong, and Rodrigo deflected, though the question unsettled him for days.

What disturbs Rodrigo most deeply is not the hypervigilance itself but the meaning he has constructed around the event. He has arrived at the quiet, corrosive belief that something about him - something he cannot fully name but is certain is real - invited what happened. He replays the moments before the officers approached, searching for what he said, how he moved, what his face communicated. He is convinced there is an answer he has not yet found. Alongside this sits a pervasive sense of isolation that he describes not as loneliness but as a kind of categorical separation from other people - as though the event placed him on the other side of a membrane through which ordinary life is visible but unreachable. His divorce, finalised three years before the incident, had already left him living alone; now the apartment feels less like solitude and more like quarantine. He has said, carefully and without drama, that he is no longer certain his life holds enough value to sustain the effort of living it.

What finally brought Rodrigo to seek help was a moment two weeks ago when a colleague showed him a photograph of a minor workplace injury - a cut across someone's palm - and Rodrigo had to leave the room. Standing in the corridor, shaking, he understood that he could no longer manage this alone. He came to the intake not with hope exactly, but with a kind of exhausted willingness - and with the fear, held close, that any exploration of what happened would only confirm what he already suspected about himself.
